newsitem.title: USA: Hilton wins okay for Missouri riverboat.
newsitem.headline: Hilton wins okay for Missouri riverboat.

text.p: Hilton Hotels Corp., one of the country's largest hoteliers, said Friday the Missouri Gaming Commission has granted Hilton a license to operate its $115 million Flamingo Casino-Kansas City riverboat on the Missouri River.

Beverly Hills, Calif.-based Hilton had planned to begin operations at the Flamingo this summer but hit a snag when Missouri regulators launched an inquiry into a $250,000 grant from Hilton to a local nonprofit organisation.

The investigation threatened to tarnish Hilton's sparkling image in the gambling industry and stall its $3 billion acquisition of Bally Entertainment Corp., which will make it the largest hotel and gambling company in the United States.
Friday's license approval ends the Missouri Gaming Commission's inquiry and allowed Hilton to open its riverboat for gambling.
"We are delighted to have completed this process and now look forward to getting on with the important work of generating revenues," Hilton Chief Executive Stephen Bollenbach said in a statement.
The Flamingo-Kansas City employs roughly 900 people and the boat contains 30,000 square feet of casino space, more than 1,000 slot machines and 60 table games.
By mid-1997, Hilton expects to have a 260-room Hilton Garden Inn operating at the riverboat complex.
The entire development would have suffered a severe setback had the Missouri Gaming Commission chosen to deny Hilton a license and continue its investigation.

Moreover, gambling regulators in states such as Nevada and New Jersey could have postponed votes on Hilton's deal with Bally. The deal, which was struck in June, has received shareholder approval and is expected to close by the end of the year.
On Thursday, Mississippi approved the merger.

The inquiry stemmed from the grant to a local organisation called K.C. Perspectives which runs business seminars for minority women. The group is headed by a former employee and business associate of Elbert Anderson, who was chairman of the Kansas City Port Authority when Hilton was negotiating terms of building a riverboat complex there.
Under its initial agreement, Hilton pledged to grant money to local non-profit groups, but only after opening the casino.

Last week in a hearing before the gaming commission, Bollenbach acknowledged Hilton made errors in handling the matter and pledged another $250,000 to the total pool available for non-profit groups. He also announced the resignation of three top officials, including former Hilton Hotels President Raymond Avansino.
The commission then voted to recommend Hilton as suitable for a license. On Thursday, regulators made their final inspection of the riverboat.
